items.title: Registering a new animal
items.question: How do I add an animal?
alternatives: how do I register a calf
items.answer: Create one permanent animal identity with the required identity, acquisition, pedigree and operational facts, then verify the saved record before recording any event against it.
items.explanation: The permanent identity is the anchor for everything that follows: milk, feed, health, vaccination, breeding, finance and exit all attach to it. DairyOS does not store the herd category directly; it derives the category from the animal's lifecycle status and sex, so those two fields decide how the animal is counted. A milking animal registered without a stated milking frequency defaults to TWICE_DAILY, and supplying a frequency for an animal that is not currently Milking is rejected outright rather than quietly ignored.

scenario.given: A new animal enters a fictional herd.
steps: Confirm identity and check for duplicate risk.
Enter the required identity and acquisition facts, including sex and lifecycle status.
Provide a milking frequency only if the animal is currently Milking.
Save, then reload the record.
Verify the passport and the resulting category.
scenario.expected: One attributable animal authority exists, its category derived from lifecycle status and sex, ready for later milk, feed, health, vaccination, breeding and exit records.
scenario.next: Record only events that actually occur.

exceptions.condition: A milking frequency is supplied for an animal that is not Milking.
exceptions.behaviour: The registration is rejected with HTTP 422. Frequency applies only to an animal currently classified as Milking.

exceptions.condition: A milking animal is registered with no frequency.
exceptions.behaviour: TWICE_DAILY is applied as the default.

exceptions.condition: Sex and lifecycle status contradict each other.
exceptions.behaviour: The registration is rejected. See animals.lifecycle for the permitted pairings.

items.correction_path: Correct identity fields through the supported edit path, which preserves the permanent identity. Never register a second animal to fix a field on the first.
items.safety: Do not register a duplicate to work around a data-entry problem; duplicate identities fragment every downstream history.

perspectives.operator: Get sex and lifecycle status right at entry, because they decide the category.
perspectives.supervisor: Duplicate identities are the most expensive registration error to unwind later.
perspectives.finance: A purchased animal has a matching Finance transaction; registration itself records no cost.
perspectives.veterinary_health: Registration creates the record that health and vaccination history will attach to.
perspectives.technical: Category is derived by AnimalClassificationService from lifecycle_status and sex, never stored independently.
perspectives.training: Register a fictional animal such as EX-COW-020 and observe the derived category.
perspectives.troubleshooting: If the category is not what you expected, check the lifecycle status rather than looking for a category field.

items.title: Lifecycle status and how the herd category is derived
items.question: How does an animal change operational status, and how is its herd category decided?
alternatives: why is this animal a Heifer
items.answer: Record the actual lifecycle event with its effective date and reason. The permanent identity and all history are retained rather than deleted, and the herd category is derived from the lifecycle status together with the animal's sex.
items.explanation: DairyOS recognises nine lifecycle statuses: CALF, HEIFER, CLOSE_UP, LACTATING, DRY, BULL, SOLD, CULLED and DECEASED. The category follows from the status and the sex. LACTATING gives Milking; DRY gives Dry; HEIFER or CLOSE_UP gives Heifer; BULL gives Bull; a CALF gives Male Calf or Female Calf according to sex; and SOLD, CULLED or DECEASED all give the derived category Exited, presented as Sold, Culled or Deceased. Certain pairings are impossible and are rejected rather than silently corrected: a male animal cannot be LACTATING, DRY or CLOSE_UP, and a female animal cannot hold BULL status. One legacy pairing is normalised, since historical records used HEIFER for male animals and that combination resolves to BULL.

scenario.given: Fictional cow EX-COW-020 is sold and leaves the herd.
steps: Confirm identity and the authority for the change.
Enter the effective date and the disposition facts.
Save, then inspect the exit history.
Verify downstream operational eligibility and the passport.
scenario.expected: The lifecycle status becomes SOLD and the derived category becomes Exited, presented as Sold. Production, health, breeding and financial history all remain traceable under the same permanent identity.
scenario.next: Reconcile any milk, sale, treatment or breeding entries around the effective date.

persisted: lifecycle status with its effective date and reason
audit: animal passport lifecycle history retained in full

exceptions.condition: A male animal is given LACTATING, DRY or CLOSE_UP.
exceptions.behaviour: Rejected. The combination is biologically invalid.

exceptions.condition: A female animal is given BULL.
A male animal carries the legacy HEIFER status.
exceptions.behaviour: Normalised to BULL, because historical records used HEIFER for males and that is semantically wrong.
It is never deleted. The identity and every linked history are retained and the animal becomes Exited.

items.correction_path: Record a further authorised lifecycle event with its own effective date. An explicit operator-supplied biological fact is never silently overwritten by canonicalisation.
items.safety: Never delete an animal to remove it from the herd. Deletion destroys the production, health, breeding and financial evidence attached to it.

perspectives.operator: Record what happened and when. The category follows on its own.
perspectives.supervisor: An exit dated wrongly moves an animal in or out of a period's totals.
perspectives.finance: A sale has a matching Finance transaction; the lifecycle event alone records no revenue.
perspectives.veterinary_health: CULLED and DECEASED are distinct outcomes and should not be used interchangeably.
perspectives.technical: AnimalClassificationService.classify derives the category from lifecycle_status and sex and rejects invalid pairings.
perspectives.training: Work a fictional animal through CALF, HEIFER, LACTATING, DRY and SOLD, and note the category at each step.
perspectives.troubleshooting: If herd totals shift unexpectedly, look for a lifecycle change with an effective date inside the period.

items.title: Herd categories and herd totals
items.question: How are herd totals calculated, and what are the herd categories?
items.answer: Herd totals are derived by classifying every active animal into one of six categories and counting them. Use the governed population for any operational calculation rather than an informal headcount.
items.explanation: DairyOS keeps a deliberate distinction between what is stored and what is displayed. The category persisted on an individual animal is singular: Milking, Dry, Heifer, Female Calf, Male Calf or Bull. The plural forms are presentation labels used for aggregate populations, translated at the herd, dashboard and report boundaries: Milking Cows, Dry Cows, Heifers, Female Calves, Male Calves and Bulls. A plural is therefore never a category an individual animal holds, and the singular is never a herd-total heading. Animals whose lifecycle status is SOLD, CULLED or DECEASED fall outside the six and are classified as Exited, so they leave the active totals without leaving the record.

scenario.given: A fictional herd contains one lactating cow, one dry cow and one male calf.
steps: Verify the affected animal identities and their lifecycle statuses.
Apply any authorised group or status change.
Refresh the dependent feed, milk and dashboard views.
Check the audit evidence and the effective date.
scenario.expected: The herd totals read Milking Cows 1, Dry Cows 1, Male Calves 1, and the animals themselves hold the singular categories Milking, Dry and Male Calf.
scenario.next: Review TMR cost and production metrics after any change to the population.

persisted: nothing; categories and totals are both derived
projected: feed category grouping and TMR cost
audit: traceable to each animal's lifecycle status and sex

exceptions.condition: An informal headcount disagrees with the system total.
exceptions.behaviour: The governed population is authoritative for calculation. Investigate the individual records.
It is categorised as Exited and drops out of the six active totals while its history remains.

items.correction_path: Correct the animal's lifecycle status or sex. Categories and totals recompute; neither is edited directly.
items.safety: Do not substitute an informal headcount for the governed population in a cost or production calculation.

perspectives.operator: The categories follow from each animal's status; you do not set them by hand.
perspectives.supervisor: If a total looks wrong, the cause is an individual animal's lifecycle status.
perspectives.finance: Herd composition drives feed category cost and therefore cost of production.
perspectives.veterinary_health: Group composition matters for treatment and vaccination planning.
perspectives.technical: CATEGORY_ORDER holds the six singular categories; CATEGORY_PLURALS maps each to its aggregate label.
perspectives.training: Write the six singular categories and their six plural labels side by side; the pairing is exact.
perspectives.troubleshooting: A total that will not reconcile usually contains an animal with an unexpected lifecycle status.

items.title: The animal passport
items.question: What is the animal passport and how do I check an animal is correctly linked?
items.answer: The passport is the per-animal view of everything recorded under one permanent identity. Use that identity as the authority, then inspect identity, lifecycle, milk, health, vaccination, breeding, lineage and exit history together.
items.explanation: Every operational domain writes back to the passport, which makes it the place where a fragmented or duplicated identity becomes visible. Because the permanent identity is the anchor and mutable labels such as ear tag or name are not, a history that looks incomplete is usually attached to a second identity rather than missing. Merging or deleting records is never the remedy, since both destroy the evidence needed to work out what happened.

scenario.given: A record for fictional cow EX-COW-020 appears duplicated or incomplete.
steps: Search by the permanent identity and the ear tag.
Compare status and the key identity fields.
Open the passport and inspect the linked histories.
Do not merge or delete records without an authorised correction path.
scenario.expected: A suspected orphan or duplicate is investigated across every linked surface before any amendment is made.
scenario.next: Raise a controlled correction with evidence and operator attribution.

persisted: nothing; the passport is a view
audit: every domain's records remain visible under the identity

exceptions.behaviour: Check for a second identity holding it before concluding records were lost.

exceptions.condition: Two records appear to be the same animal.
exceptions.behaviour: Escalate. Do not merge them yourself.

items.correction_path: Correct through the workflow that owns the record. The passport reflects the correction and retains what preceded it.
items.safety: Never merge or delete animal records to tidy an apparent duplicate. Escalate with evidence instead.

perspectives.operator: The passport is where you check you are looking at the right animal.
perspectives.supervisor: It is the fastest way to spot a duplicate identity.
perspectives.finance: Purchase and sale transactions appear against the animal's history.
perspectives.veterinary_health: Health, treatment, withdrawal and vaccination history all surface here.
perspectives.technical: The passport aggregates across domains keyed on the permanent identity.
perspectives.training: Open a fictional animal's passport and name the domain that wrote each section.
perspectives.troubleshooting: Missing history is far more often a second identity than a lost record.

items.title: Finding the right animal
items.question: How should an animal be located safely?
items.answer: Search by the permanent identity and corroborating identity fields, then confirm the passport before recording or amending anything.
items.explanation: Almost every serious data error in an operational system begins with an event attached to the wrong animal, and that error is expensive because it is invisible at the moment it is made. Confirming the passport before writing costs seconds; unwinding a misattributed treatment, breeding event or milk record afterwards touches every domain that consumed it.

scenario.given: An operator needs to act on an animal in a fictional herd.
steps: Search by permanent identity, ear tag or another approved identifier.
Compare name, status and identity details.
Open the passport to confirm the target.
Only then choose the operational workflow.
scenario.expected: The event attaches to the correct animal and duplicate identities are avoided.
scenario.next: Report conflicting identity evidence before writing any record.

derived: the identified animal for the next workflow
projected: correct cross-domain linkage of whatever is recorded next

exceptions.behaviour: Stop and resolve the identity before recording anything.

exceptions.condition: The ear tag matches but other details do not.
exceptions.behaviour: Trust the permanent identity, not the label, and report the conflict.

items.correction_path: No correction is needed for a search. If an event was recorded against the wrong animal, correct it through that domain's own workflow.
items.safety: Confirm the animal before writing. A misattributed record is far harder to undo than to prevent.

perspectives.operator: Check the passport before you enter anything.
perspectives.supervisor: Most cross-domain data problems begin with a wrong-animal entry.
perspectives.veterinary_health: A treatment recorded against the wrong animal puts the wrong milk under withdrawal.
perspectives.technical: Search supports permanent identity, ear tag and other approved identifiers.
perspectives.training: Search a fictional herd by tag and by identity and compare what each returns.
perspectives.troubleshooting: If results look wrong, search by permanent identity rather than a mutable label.

items.title: Correcting an animal's identity details
items.question: How should an animal identity correction be made?
items.answer: Use the supported edit path, keep the permanent identity unchanged, record the reason and who made the change, then verify every linked surface afterwards.
items.explanation: Identity fields such as ear tag, name and breed are labels attached to a permanent identity, and correcting them must not create a new one. This matters because every other domain refers to the permanent identity: change that and the histories orphan, while changing only the label leaves them intact. A correction is recorded with its reason so that a later reader can tell a genuine correction from a transcription error repeated.

scenario.given: An ear tag or profile field is incorrect for fictional cow EX-COW-020.
steps: Capture the current identity and the evidence for the change.
Edit only the authorised field.
Save and reload the animal.
Check the passport, milk, health, vaccination, breeding and lifecycle links.
scenario.expected: The correction is traceable and no dependent history is orphaned.
scenario.next: Escalate if the permanent identity itself appears duplicated.

persisted: the corrected field, its reason and attribution
derived: updated presentation of the animal across surfaces
audit: prior value retained in the audit trail

exceptions.condition: The permanent identity itself is wrong.
exceptions.behaviour: That is not an edit. Escalate, because it may indicate a duplicate.

exceptions.condition: The change would alter sex or lifecycle status.
exceptions.behaviour: Those are not identity labels. They change the derived category, so use the lifecycle workflow.

items.correction_path: Edits are themselves the correction path, and each one is recorded with its reason.
items.safety: Never change the permanent identity to fix a label. That orphans every linked history.

perspectives.operator: Fix the tag, not the animal's identity.
perspectives.supervisor: The reason field distinguishes a real correction from a repeated mistake.
perspectives.veterinary_health: A changed tag must not break the link to treatment and withdrawal history.
perspectives.technical: The permanent identity is immutable; identity fields are mutable labels over it.
perspectives.training: Change a fictional animal's ear tag and confirm its histories still resolve.
perspectives.troubleshooting: If history disappears after an edit, the permanent identity was altered rather than a label.

items.title: Setting an animal's milking frequency
items.question: How do I set or change how often an animal is milked?
items.answer: Milking frequency is a dated property of the animal and applies only while it is classified as Milking. DairyOS accepts TWICE_DAILY or THRICE_DAILY, and a milking animal registered without one defaults to TWICE_DAILY.
items.explanation: Frequency is held as dated history rather than a single current value, so each production date is judged against the frequency effective on that date. Changing it today therefore does not rewrite what was expected last week. Supplying a frequency for an animal that is not currently Milking is rejected with HTTP 422, because the concept has no meaning for a dry cow, a heifer, a calf or a bull. Which sessions the frequency then expects is covered by milk.session-plan.

scenario.given: Fictional cow EX-COW-020 is Milking on TWICE_DAILY and is moved to THRICE_DAILY from a stated date.
steps: Confirm the animal is currently classified as Milking.
Record the new frequency with its effective date.
Verify the dated frequency history.
Check which sessions are now expected from that date onward.
scenario.expected: Dates before the change still expect MORNING and EVENING; dates from the change onward expect MORNING, AFTERNOON and EVENING. Earlier days are not retrospectively incomplete.
scenario.next: Enter milk against the sessions the effective frequency expects.

derived: expected sessions for each production date

exceptions.condition: The animal is not classified as Milking.
exceptions.behaviour: Rejected with HTTP 422. Milking frequency applies only to an animal currently classified as Milking.

exceptions.condition: The value is not a governed frequency.
exceptions.behaviour: Rejected. Only TWICE_DAILY and THRICE_DAILY are accepted.

exceptions.condition: A Milking animal is registered with no frequency.
exceptions.behaviour: TWICE_DAILY is applied as the default.

items.correction_path: Record a further dated frequency change. Earlier dates keep the expectation that was effective for them.
items.safety: Do not change frequency to resolve a historical completeness problem; it does not rewrite past expectations, and it should not.

perspectives.operator: Set it from the date the change actually takes effect.
perspectives.supervisor: A frequency change alters expected sessions from that date onward only.
perspectives.finance: More sessions may mean more litres, which moves the cost per litre denominator.
perspectives.veterinary_health: Frequency changes are management decisions and are recorded separately from health records.
perspectives.technical: Only TWICE_DAILY and THRICE_DAILY are governed values; the dated history is what completeness reads.
perspectives.training: Change a fictional animal's frequency mid-period and check that earlier days are unaffected.
perspectives.troubleshooting: If a past day suddenly looks incomplete, check whether a frequency change was dated too early.
